description: Hi, we're an interdisciplinary team from the far North of the globe! We focus on user-centric design and making sure the farmers get the most of our product.
summary:
As climate conditions change rapidly, crop selection is becoming increasingly unclear. Crops once well established in certain regions now face greater susceptibility to sudden shifts in climate and precipitation patterns, such as those driven by the 2026 super El Niño event, which risks mass crop failures worldwide. Pocketbook is a device designed to help alleviate the burden of navigating such uncertain year-to-year conditions for farmers worldwide. Through it, we aim to create a decision-support platform that lets farmers make informed choices based on rapidly shifting conditions and the best-performing crops and varieties. 
After some research, we defined resilience as an agricultural system’s adaptability, robustness, and transformability. One of our main approaches was creating a system that allowed logging and scheduling of crop rotations. Crop rotations are already used worldwide, and giving farmers more flexibility to plan them in a changing climate could help secure harvests during years when the climate proves erratic. These options are documented through the crop almanac, a Pocketbook feature that catalogs crop varieties and shows not only a variety’s characteristics (drought tolerance, nitrogen usage) but also recommends hand-picked rotation partners for that crop. 
Pocketbook also serves as a data visualization tool, displaying meteorological data received from NASA. Through its soil probe, it can also record and store data directly from a farm plot.
details:
Farmers' best friend during changing climates

We seek to explore one question: How might we inform farmers of when to plant and what to plant so that they could navigate changing climates and agricultural systems better?

How it works

The Pocketbook maps meteorological datasets from NASA (such as their live weather data) to agronomic datasets from other research institutes (such as Soybean Research and Information Network) to form timely crop advice to farmers so they could practice crop rotation more efficiently. The device also operates with a plugged in soil pH sensor and a humidity sensor to collect real-time data of farmers' own fields.

Impact

The demand for climate service devices will only keep growing as the world struggles to adapt to ecological crises. From our interviews with agronomists at NGOs and research institution, we concluded that a decision-support device that could give concrete, actionable advices on crops to farmers would have much impact on helping them securing the planting windows.

Tools used

Figma/Figjam: Design + Prototyping

Framer: Website

Blender: hardware concept

Creative decisions

1. A physical device instead of an app: After talking to agronomists around the world, we realized not all farmers use smartphones, and a lot of them don't bring smartphones to the field. A physical device was chosen because it could be made to be weather resistant, making assessing soil less of a hassle.

2. Emphasising explanation and transparency. Weather forecasting is inevitably wrong at one point. It is more important that we provide farmers the explanation of why we decided to advise them to do a certain thing so they could judge for themselves. We recognized that a split-screen device could provide a lot more contextual information to farmers.

3. We utilised what we have. Our team consists of one agronomist and one designers, so we emphasised on our deliberate understanding of the end users and the entire communication chain that binds them together.
